transcript.content: Hello, I am Dr. Smith. Could you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. I’ve completely lost interest in the design work and hobbies that usually keep me grounded, and I can’t seem to care about anything right now. It just feels like I've run completely out of steam and I don't know what to do.
Have you experienced similar periods of feeling this low in the past, and if so, how long have these low moods typically lasted?

Yes, these heavy lows have been happening off and on for about a year, especially since my spouse and I separated. This current low has been dragging on for close to a year, but it's gotten so much worse and harder to manage over the last month.
During the past year, have there been any periods of several months where you felt completely back to your normal self, or has your mood been consistently low for most of that time?

I haven't really had any periods of feeling normal over the past year. Instead, I've either been stuck in this heavy, dragging low, or I'm in one of those overly revved-up, intense cycles where I feel like I'm running on overdrive. It has just been one extreme or the other without much of a middle ground.
During those 'revved-up' periods, how long do they typically last, and have they ever been intense enough to significantly disrupt your work or require medical attention?

Those revved-up periods usually last anywhere from several days to a couple of weeks, and they've never required medical attention—most people at work just thought I was "hustling." However, I did make some impulsive financial decisions during them, like booking an expensive solo trip and putting money into a friend's sketchy startup, which I'm really stressing about now.

Looking back at your life before this past year, have you ever experienced distinct periods of these 'revved-up' moods or extreme lows that lasted for several years, even if they weren't as severe as they are now?

No, I don't recall having these kinds of extreme highs and lows before this past year. These distinct cycles of feeling revved up and then crashing really only started happening about a year ago, around the time my spouse and I separated.
During those 'revved-up' periods, did you notice a decreased need for sleep, like feeling fully rested after only a few hours, or were you just feeling more energetic than usual?

Yes, absolutely. During those phases, I would sleep for only three or four hours a night but wake up feeling completely sharp and energized. I actually felt almost annoyed that I had to waste any time sleeping at all.

During those revved-up periods, did your behavior ever become so extreme that it caused significant problems at work or in your personal relationships, or did you ever experience any hallucinations or delusions?

During those times, I did snap at people who told me to tone down my intensity, and the impulsive decisions like booking that expensive trip and investing in a sketchy startup have caused me major financial stress. But as for hallucinations or delusions, no, I have never experienced anything like that.
During those revved-up periods, did your behavior reach a point where you were unable to function at work or perform your daily responsibilities for at least four consecutive days?

No, during those revved-up times I actually felt the opposite—I was extremely sharp and overly productive, taking on tons of extra work and social commitments. While I made some impulsive financial decisions, the actual inability to function and manage my daily responsibilities only happened after I crashed into this low period.
During those 'revved-up' periods, did they last for at least four consecutive days, even if you were still able to function or were even more productive than usual?

Yes, those revved-up periods definitely lasted longer than four days, typically going on for a couple of weeks at a time. During those weeks, I felt incredibly sharp, highly productive, and active even though I was only sleeping three or four hours a night.

I have included F32.9 (unspecified depressive episode), F33.9 (recurrent depressive disorder), and F34.1 (dysthymia) as initial candidates to distinguish between acute, recurrent, or chronic presentations. Further questioning is needed to assess duration, severity, and associated physical symptoms.

The patient reports a persistent low mood for approximately one year, which aligns with both chronic depressive states (F34.1) and potentially recurrent episodes (F33.9). Given the recent exacerbation, a major depressive episode (F32.9) is also a strong candidate. I need to determine if there were distinct periods of remission or if the mood has been consistently low for the entire year to differentiate between these possibilities.
